claim: Approximately 10 million people are infected with tuberculosis each year.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), with approximately 10 million people being infected each year and 1.6 million deaths in 2021 (Furin et al., 2019; Bagcchi, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Furin et al., 2019 and Bagcchi, 2023.

claim: There were 1.6 million tuberculosis deaths in 2021.
source: Tuberculosis (TB) is a chronic infectious disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), with approximately 10 million people being infected each year and 1.6 million deaths in 2021 (Furin et al., 2019; Bagcchi, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Furin et al., 2019 and Bagcchi, 2023.

claim: Global spending on essential TB services for TB diagnosis, treatment, and prevention has exceeded $6.4 billion.
source: According to the World Health Organization (WHO) Global TB Report 2022, the global spending on essential TB services for TB diagnosis, treatment, and prevention has exceeded $6.4 billion (Global tuberculosis report 2023, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to the WHO Global TB Report 2022.

claim: Drug-resistant forms of Mtb are responsible for a quarter of deaths due to antimicrobial resistance.
source: Besides, drug-resistant forms of Mtb are currently on course to be the world's deadliest pathogens, responsible for a quarter of deaths due to antimicrobial resistance (Furin et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Furin et al., 2019.

claim: Intestinal microbiota dysbiosis may affect the occurrence and development of respiratory diseases including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and respiratory pathogens infection by the 'gut–lung axis'.
source: Some studies have shown that intestinal microbiota dysbiosis may affect the occurrence and development of respiratory diseases including asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, respiratory pathogens infection, etc. by the 'gut–lung axis' (Keely et al., 2012; Barcik et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Keely et al., 2012; Barcik et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023.

claim: The abundance of Prevotellaceae and Enterococcaceae was increased in pediatric pulmonary TB patients compared with healthy control subjects.
source: A case–control study of pulmonary TB in pediatric patients showed that the abundance of Prevotellaceae and Enterococcaceae was increased, and the abundance of Oscillospiraceae and Bifidobacteriaceae was decreased in TB patients compared with healthy control subjects (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: The abundance of Oscillospiraceae and Bifidobacteriaceae was decreased in pediatric pulmonary TB patients compared with healthy control subjects.
source: A case–control study of pulmonary TB in pediatric patients showed that the abundance of Prevotellaceae and Enterococcaceae was increased, and the abundance of Oscillospiraceae and Bifidobacteriaceae was decreased in TB patients compared with healthy control subjects (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2019.

claim: The levels of Prevotella decreased and Bacteroides increased in TB patients.
source: Maji et al. have found that the levels of Provetalla decreased and Bacteroides increased in TB patients (Maji et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maji et al., 2018.

claim: The abundance of Bacteroidetes significantly altered in active TB patients compared with health subjects.
source: Recently, our teams' study in active TB patients showed the abundance of Bacteroidetes significantly altered compared with health subjects (Han et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Han et al., 2024.

claim: The phylum of Bacteroidetes altered in the feces samples of patients with recurrent TB.
source: Another study also showed the phylum of Bacteroidetes altered in the feces samples of patients with recurrent TB (Luo et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Luo et al., 2017.

claim: Alcohol, smoking, HIV infection, and diabetes cause gut microbiota dysbiosis and are important risk factors for TB.
source: Some factors including alcohol, smoking, HIV infection, and diabetes have been proven to cause gut microbiota dysbiosis, and these also are important risk factors for TB (Naidoo et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Naidoo et al., 2019.

claim: Mice fed with a high-fat diet-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis increased the risk of developing active TB in mice.
source: A recent study has shown that the mice fed with a high-fat diet-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis increased the risk of developing active TB in mice (Arias et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Arias et al., 2019.

claim: Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio increased in a murine model of type 2 diabetes induced by an energy-dense diet and increased the susceptibility to Mtb infection.
source: Another study found Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes ratio increased in a murine model of type 2 diabetes induced by an energy-dense diet, and increased the susceptibility to Mtb infection (Sathkumara et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Sathkumara et al., 2021.

claim: Clindamycin is an antibiotic that selectively disorders anaerobic Bacteroidetes.
source: Hence, in the present study, clindamycin (CL), an antibiotic that selectively disorders anaerobic Bacteroidetes (You et al., 2019), was used to establish a mouse model of intestinal microbiota dysbiosis.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to You et al., 2019.

claim: Clindamycin treatment significantly increased Mycobacterium smegmatis colonization in the lungs of mice compared to control mice.
source: The results showed that the mice with clindamycin treated presented a significantly higher colonization of MS in the lungs than that of control mice (Figure 1b, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The cecum of CL-treated mice was markedly more dilated compared with the control groups.
source: The size of the cecum of CL-treated mice was markedly more dilated compared with the control groups (Figure 1c, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The levels of i-FABP were significantly higher in the CL group than in the control group.
source: The results showed that the levels of i-FABP and LPS were significantly higher in the CL group than in the control group (CON) (Figure 1d, e, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: The levels of LPS were significantly higher in the CL group than in the control group.
source: The results showed that the levels of i-FABP and LPS were significantly higher in the CL group than in the control group (CON) (Figure 1d, e, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Intestinal epithelial tissues of mice showed no obvious alteration after clindamycin treatment versus the control group.
source: Pathological sections of intestinal tissue showed the intestinal epithelial tissues of mice with no obvious alteration after clindamycin treatment vs the CON group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was more diffused inflammation and inflammatory cell infiltration in the CL-treated mice compared with the control group after infecting with MS.
source: H&E staining of paraffin-embedded lung sections revealed that there was more diffused inflammation and inflammatory cell infiltration in the CL-treated mice compared with that of the CON group animals after infecting with MS (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: CL treatment damages the enterocyte, increases gut permeability, promotes the fermentation of cecum contents, and increases MS colonization in the lungs of mice.
source: All these results indicated that CL treatment damages the enterocyte, increases gut permeability, promotes the fermentation of cecum contents, and increases MS colonization in the lungs of mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results including i-FABP, LPS levels, cecum size, and MS colonization data.

claim: The α-diversity of gut bacterial microbiota was significantly decreased in the CL group compared with the CON group.
source: For the gut bacterial analysis, the α-diversity was significantly decreased in the CL group compared with the CON group (Figure 2a, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The intestinal bacterial microbial community structure was significantly different between the CL-treated mice and the control mice.
source: The β-diversity based on the weighted UniFrac distance showed that the CL group samples were separated from the CON group (R = 0.8488, p = 0.001) (Figure 2b). It indicated that the intestinal bacterial microbial community structure was a significant difference between the CL-treated mice and the control mice.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b with statistical significance (R = 0.8488, p = 0.001).

claim: The CL group had a remarkable decrease of Bacteroidota and a significant increase of Firmicutes and Proteobacteria compared to the control group at the phylum level.
source: At the phylum level, we observed a remarkable decrease of Bacteroidota and a significant increase of Firmicutes and Proteobacteria in the CL group compared to the control group (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The CL group had a significantly higher relative abundance of Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, Escherichia–Shigella, and Faecalibaculum compared with the CON group at the genus level.
source: At the genus level, the CL group had a significantly higher relative abundance of Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, Escherichia–Shigella, and Faecalibaculum, and a lower abundance of Dubosiella, Alloprevotella, Akkermansia, and Bifidobacterium compared with that in the CON group (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The CL group had a lower abundance of Dubosiella, Alloprevotella, Akkermansia, and Bifidobacterium compared with the CON group at the genus level.
source: At the genus level, the CL group had a significantly higher relative abundance of Bacteroides, Lactobacillus, Escherichia–Shigella, and Faecalibaculum, and a lower abundance of Dubosiella, Alloprevotella, Akkermansia, and Bifidobacterium compared with that in the CON group (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The Chao1 and inverse Simpson indices of gut fungal mycobiota in the CL group was significantly increased compared to that of the CON group.
source: For the fungal mycobiota analysis, the Chao1 and inverse Simpson indices of the CL group was significantly increased compared to that of the CON group (Figure 2a).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The community of intestinal mycobiota in the CL and CON groups is different.
source: The principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) showed that the samples were significantly distinguished between two groups (R = 0.6038, p = 0.001) (Figure 2b), which suggested that the community of intestinal mycobiota in the two groups is different.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b with statistical significance (R = 0.6038, p = 0.001).

claim: The relative abundance of Basidiomycota significantly increases in the CL group compared with the CON group.
source: At the phylum level, the fungal microbiota was dominated by the Ascomycota and Basidiomycota in two groups, and Ascomycota showed no obvious differences between the two groups. However, the relative abundance of Basidiomycota significantly increases in the CL group compared with the CON group (Figure 2c, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2c and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The relative abundance of Aspergillus, Penicillium, Cladosporium, and Alternaria was enriched in the CL group versus the CON group at the genus level.
source: The LEfSe analysis at the genus level showed that the relative abundance of Aspergillus, Penicillium, Cladosporium, and Alternaria was enriched in the CL group vs the CON group (Figure 2d, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2d and Supplementary file 1.

claim: CL treatment altered the diversity and composition of the intestinal microbiome (including bacterial and fungi) in the mice and induced gut microbiome dysbiosis.
source: Taken together, all these data indicated that CL treatment altered the diversity and composition of the intestinal microbiome (including bacterial and fungi) in the mice and induced gut microbiome dysbiosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results on bacterial and fungal microbiome diversity and composition.

claim: The ITS/16S ratio of the CL group was significantly increased compared with the CON group.
source: The results show that the ITS/16S ratio of the CL group was significantly increased compared with the CON group (Figure 3a, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The ratio of Firmicutes/Bacteroidota in the CL group was increased compared with that of the CON group.
source: The results showed that the ratio of Firmicutes/Bacteroidota in the CL group was increased, and Ascomycota/Basidiomycota was significantly decreased compared with that of the CON group (Figure 3b, c, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The ratio of Ascomycota/Basidiomycota was significantly decreased in the CL group compared with that of the CON group.
source: The results showed that the ratio of Firmicutes/Bacteroidota in the CL group was increased, and Ascomycota/Basidiomycota was significantly decreased compared with that of the CON group (Figure 3b, c, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: In the control group, bacteria and fungi were closely related to each other, gathering in a cluster and forming a more complex network.
source: In the control group, the bacteria and fungi were closely related to each other, gathering in a cluster and forming a more complex network (Figure 3d).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The control group trans-kingdom network had 154 nodes including 45 fungi and 109 bacteria, and 810 edges with relative connectedness of 5.26.
source: There were 154 nodes including 45 fungi and 109 bacteria, and 810 edges; the relative connectedness was 5.26 (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis data shown in Table 1.

claim: The complexity of the trans-kingdom network in the CL group was dramatically decreased compared to the control group.
source: However, the complexity of the trans-kingdom network in the CL group was dramatically decreased, and the interplay between bacteria and fungi was also weakened (Figure 3e).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The CL group trans-kingdom network had 110 nodes including 62 fungi and 48 bacteria with 357 edges and relative connectedness of 3.25.
source: A total of 110 nodes including 62 fungi and 48 bacteria gathered into clusters in this network. The edges decreased to 357 and the relative connectedness was 3.25 in the CL group network (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis data shown in Table 1.

claim: The interplay ratio between fungi in the CL group was 52.10%, which was much higher than that of the CON group (7.53%).
source: We also found that the interplay ratio between fungi in the CL group was 52.10%, which was much higher than that of the CON group (7.53%) (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis data shown in Table 1.

claim: Clindamycin treatment not only altered the proportion of bacteria and fungi, but also weakened the trans-kingdom networks, changed the interactions between bacteria and fungi, and resulted in gut microbiome dysbiosis.
source: All these results indicated that clindamycin treatment not only altered the proportion of bacteria and fungi, but also weakened the trans-kingdom networks, changed the interactions between bacteria and fungi, and resulted in gut microbiome dysbiosis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results on trans-kingdom network analysis.

claim: The α-diversity of gut bacterial microbiota was significantly decreased in the CL-FMT group compared with the CON-FMT group.
source: The results show that the α-diversity of gut bacterial microbiota was significantly decreased, and the α-diversity of gut fungal microbiota was significantly increased in the CL-FMT group compared with that in the CON-FMT group (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The α-diversity of gut fungal microbiota was significantly increased in the CL-FMT group compared with the CON-FMT group.
source: The results show that the α-diversity of gut bacterial microbiota was significantly decreased, and the α-diversity of gut fungal microbiota was significantly increased in the CL-FMT group compared with that in the CON-FMT group (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a significant separation of gut bacterial and fungal microbiota between CL-FMT and CON-FMT recipient samples.
source: The results show a significant separation of gut bacterial and fungal microbiota between CT- and AD-recipient samples (p = 0.007 and p = 0.042, Figure 4b).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4b with statistical significance (p = 0.007 and p = 0.042).

claim: The fungal-to-bacterial species ratio was significantly increased in the CL-FMT versus the CON-FMT recipient groups.
source: The fungal-to-bacterial species ratio was significantly increased in the CL- vs the CON-recipient groups (p < 0.05, Figure 4c, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c with statistical significance (p < 0.05).

claim: Firmicutes/Bacteroidota in the CL-FMT group was decreased compared with that of the CON-FMT group.
source: The results show that Firmicutes/Bacteroidota in the CL-FMT group was decreased, and Ascomycota/Basidiomycota was no obvious different compared with that of the CON-FMT group (Figure 4d, e, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Ascomycota/Basidiomycota showed no obvious difference between the CL-FMT and CON-FMT groups.
source: The results show that Firmicutes/Bacteroidota in the CL-FMT group was decreased, and Ascomycota/Basidiomycota was no obvious different compared with that of the CON-FMT group (Figure 4d, e, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4e.

claim: The complexity of the microbiome network was significantly reduced and the interactions between bacteria and fungi were weakened in the CL-FMT versus the CON-FMT groups.
source: The trans-kingdom network analyses between bacteria and fungi showed the complexity of the microbiome network was significantly reduced and the interactions between bacteria and fungi were also weakened in the CL-FMT vs the CON-FMT groups (Figure 4f).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis data shown in Figure 4f.

claim: 85.11% (40/47) of bacterial genera present in the CL inocula were successfully transferred to the CL-recipient mice.
source: The results showed that 85.11% (40/47) of bacterial genera and 52.38% (33/63) of fungi genera present in the CL inocula were successfully transferred to the CL-recipient mice, and 91.45% (107/117) of bacteria genera and 56.36% (31/55) of fungi genera in the CON inocula were also successfully transferred to the CON-recipient mice, respectively (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: 52.38% (33/63) of fungi genera present in the CL inocula were successfully transferred to the CL-recipient mice.
source: The results showed that 85.11% (40/47) of bacterial genera and 52.38% (33/63) of fungi genera present in the CL inocula were successfully transferred to the CL-recipient mice, and 91.45% (107/117) of bacteria genera and 56.36% (31/55) of fungi genera in the CON inocula were also successfully transferred to the CON-recipient mice, respectively (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: 91.45% (107/117) of bacteria genera in the CON inocula were successfully transferred to the CON-recipient mice.
source: The results showed that 85.11% (40/47) of bacterial genera and 52.38% (33/63) of fungi genera present in the CL inocula were successfully transferred to the CL-recipient mice, and 91.45% (107/117) of bacteria genera and 56.36% (31/55) of fungi genera in the CON inocula were also successfully transferred to the CON-recipient mice, respectively (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: 56.36% (31/55) of fungi genera in the CON inocula were successfully transferred to the CON-recipient mice.
source: The results showed that 85.11% (40/47) of bacterial genera and 52.38% (33/63) of fungi genera present in the CL inocula were successfully transferred to the CL-recipient mice, and 91.45% (107/117) of bacteria genera and 56.36% (31/55) of fungi genera in the CON inocula were also successfully transferred to the CON-recipient mice, respectively (Figure 4g).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: The FMT model was successfully established, and the CL-recipient mice showed similar characteristics of gut microbiota dysbiosis with the CL group.
source: These results indicated that the FMT model was successfully established, and the CL-recipient mice showed similar characteristics of gut microbiota dysbiosis with the CL group.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results on FMT including microbiome transfer rates and network analyses.

claim: The burden of MS in the lungs of CL-recipient mice was significantly higher than that in the CON-recipient mice after 72 hr of MS infection.
source: Then, we assessed the susceptibility of MS in the lungs of FMT mice, the results showed that the burden of MS in the lungs of CL-recipient mice was significantly rise than that in the CON-recipient mice after 72 hr of MS infection (Figure 4h, Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: The size of the cecum showed no significant differences between the CL-FMT and CON-FMT groups.
source: However, the size of the cecum showed no significant differences between the two groups (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The level of iFABP significantly increased in the CL-recipient mice compared with the CON-recipient mice after FMT.
source: The level of iFABP and LPS also significantly increased in the CL-recipient mice compared with the CON-recipient mice after FMT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The level of LPS significantly increased in the CL-recipient mice compared with the CON-recipient mice after FMT.
source: The level of iFABP and LPS also significantly increased in the CL-recipient mice compared with the CON-recipient mice after FMT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The intestinal epithelial tissues of mice have no significant damage after FMT.
source: The pathological sections of intestinal tissue showed the intestinal epithelial tissues of mice have no significant damage after FMT (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Gut microbiota dysbiosis increases intestinal permeability and enhances the susceptibility of MS colonization in the lungs of mice.
source: Altogether, our data suggested that gut microbiota dysbiosis increases intestinal permeability and enhances the susceptibility of MS colonization in the lungs of mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results from the FMT model including MS colonization, iFABP, and LPS levels.

claim: There were 1191 upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 1013 downregulated DEGs in the CL versus the CON groups.
source: The results showed that there were 1191 upregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and 1013 downregulated DEGs in the CL vs the CON groups (false discovery rate [FDR] <0.05, and fold change [FC] >1, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 274 DEGs were upregulated and 32 DEGs were downregulated in the CL-FMT group compared with the CON-FMT group.
source: Compared with the CON-FMT group, 274 DEGs were upregulated and 32 DEGs were downregulated in the CL-FMT group (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: 93 upregulating DEGs and 5 downregulating DEGs were commonly expressed between CL vs CON and CL-FMT vs CON-FMT comparisons.
source: The Venn diagram showed that 93 upregulating DEGs and 5 downregulating DEGs were commonly expressed among these groups (Figure 5a).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: CL and CL-FMT groups mainly affected the immune response and inflammatory response, including 'defense response', 'response to bacterium', 'cellular response to interleukin-1', and 'cellular response to lipopolysaccharide'.
source: The top 30 biological processes enriched by GO showed that CL and CL-FMT groups mainly affected the immune response and inflammatory response, including 'defense response', 'response to bacterium', 'cellular response to interleukin-1', and 'cellular response to lipopolysaccharide' (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The enriched molecular functions of the 98 DEGs were some cytokine and protease involving the immune defense response, including 'cytokine activity', 'chemokine activity', 'nitric-oxide synthase binding', and 'CXCR chemokine receptor binding'.
source: The enriched molecular functions of these DEGs were some cytokine and protease involving the immune defense response, including 'cytokine activity', 'chemokine activity', 'nitric-oxide synthase binding', and 'CXCR chemokine receptor binding' (Figure 5b).
evidence: The claim is supported by GO enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The 98 DEGs are mainly involved in environmental information processing, human diseases, and organismal systems at KEGG classification level 1.
source: The top 20 KEGG pathways enrichment analyses at classification level 1 indicated that these DEGs are mainly involved in environmental information processing, human diseases, and organismal systems (Figure 5c and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5c and Supplementary file 2.

claim: There were six pathways relating to infectious disease and seven pathways involving the immune system among the enrichment top 20 pathways at KEGG classification level 2.
source: At classification level 2 of the KEGG analysis, we found six pathways relating to infectious disease, and seven pathways involving the immune system among the enrichment top 20 pathways (Figure 5c and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5c and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Among the six pathways of infectious disease, there were three pathways involving bacterial infectious disease, including TB, legionellosis, and pertussis.
source: Interestingly, among the six pathways of infectious disease, there were three pathways involving bacterial infectious disease, including TB, legionellosis, and pertussis (Figure 5c).
evidence: The claim is supported by KEGG enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Eight genes were strongly associated with TB based on interaction network analysis with nine KEGG pathways related to human disease.
source: For the future screening of the potential regulatory genes correlated with TB, nine KEGG pathways related to human disease were selected for interaction network analysis with DEGs. The results showed that eight genes were strongly associated with TB (Figure 5d).
evidence: The claim is supported by network analysis shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Seven genes including Nos2, Cd14, Tnf, Cd74, Clec4e, Ctsd, and Il6 are upregulating expression in the CL and CL-FMT groups.
source: Among those genes, seven genes including Nos2, Cd14, Tnf, Cd74, Clec4e, Ctsd, and Il6 are upregulating expression and the Cd209a gene is the downregulating expression in the CL and CL-FMT groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Cd209a gene is downregulating expression in the CL and CL-FMT groups.
source: Among those genes, seven genes including Nos2, Cd14, Tnf, Cd74, Clec4e, Ctsd, and Il6 are upregulating expression and the Cd209a gene is the downregulating expression in the CL and CL-FMT groups (Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Nos2 gene was an enriched expression in both GO and KEGG analyses.
source: It is worth noting that the Nos2 gene was an enriched expression in both GO and KEGG analyses.
evidence: The claim is inferred from GO and KEGG enrichment analyses.

claim: The genes of Nos2, Ctsd, Cd74, and Tnf were increased in CL-FMT and CL groups compared with that in control groups.
source: Then, we performed an RT-qPCR to assess the validity of the transcriptome. The results revealed that the genes of Nos2, Ctsd, Cd74, and Tnf were increased in CL-FMT and CL groups compared with that in control groups (Figure 5e, Figure 5—source data 1), which indicated that the RNA-seq data is reliable.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The RNA-seq data is reliable.
source: Then, we performed an RT-qPCR to assess the validity of the transcriptome. The results revealed that the genes of Nos2, Ctsd, Cd74, and Tnf were increased in CL-FMT and CL groups compared with that in control groups (Figure 5e, Figure 5—source data 1), which indicated that the RNA-seq data is reliable.
evidence: The claim is inferred from RT-qPCR validation of RNA-seq results.

claim: Gut microbiota dysbiosis significantly altered the transcriptomic profiling in the lung tissue of mice and increased the expression of Nos2 genes.
source: In summary, our data revealed that gut microbiota dysbiosis significantly altered the transcriptomic profiling in the lung tissue of mice, and increased the expression of Nos2 genes.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple transcriptomic analyses.

claim: The expression level of Nos2 was significantly raised in A549 cells after transfection with the Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid.
source: The results showed that the expression level of Nos2 was significantly raised in A549 cells after transfection with the Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid (Figure 6a, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a.

claim: MS colonization density was significantly increased in A549 cells with Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid after infection MS 6, 12, and 24 hr.
source: MS colonization density was significantly increased in A549 cells with Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid after infection MS 6, 12, and 24 hr (Figure 6b, Figure 6—source data 1), which suggested that Nos2 overexpression increases the infection susceptibility of MS to A549 cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Nos2 overexpression increases the infection susceptibility of MS to A549 cells.
source: MS colonization density was significantly increased in A549 cells with Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid after infection MS 6, 12, and 24 hr (Figure 6b, Figure 6—source data 1), which suggested that Nos2 overexpression increases the infection susceptibility of MS to A549 cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from MS colonization data in Nos2-overexpressing cells.

claim: The NO level significantly increased in the A549 cells with transfection of the Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid.
source: The results showed that the NO level significantly increased in the A549 cells with transfection of the Nos2-pcDNA3.1 plasmid (Figure 6c, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: ROS concentration in A549 cells transfected with Nos2-pcDNA3.1 was significantly lower than that in the control A549 and A549 cells transfected with pcDNA3.1 empty vector.
source: As fluorescence microscopy shown in Figure 6d, ROS concentration in A549 cells transfected with Nos2-pcDNA3.1 was significantly lower than that in the control A549 and A549 cells transfected with pcDNA3.1 empty vector (Figure 6d, Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Nos2 overexpression significantly reduced the level of Defb1 in A549 cells.
